title: Symmetric Spaces
notes: Open by framing the chapter as a machine for recognizing spaces from point reflections. The local picture is simple, but the payoff is large: affine symmetry constrains curvature, global symmetry gives a transitive isometry group, and the tangent algebra records the whole geometry.

title: Local Symmetry Starts In Normal Coordinates
notes: Begin at one point and keep the picture deliberately local. In normal coordinates, the geodesic symmetry is just the operation that sends a tangent vector to its negative. The key question is not whether this reflection can be drawn, but whether it preserves the affine structure.

title: Affine Symmetry Leaves A Curvature Fingerprint
notes: Use this slide to connect the reflection test with tensor conditions. If each local geodesic symmetry is affine, torsion disappears and curvature is parallel. That means a measurement made at one point can be transported consistently along nearby geodesics without changing its algebraic content.

title: Global Symmetry Forces Homogeneity
notes: Shift from local data to global motion. A globally symmetric Riemannian space has point symmetries that extend to isometries, and those isometries can move the base point around the manifold. This is the conceptual reason the chapter arrives at a homogeneous model G over K.

title: The Symmetric Pair Splits The Algebra
notes: Present the involution as the algebraic shadow of a point reflection. The fixed part k is infinitesimal isotropy, while p represents tangent directions at the base point. The bracket containment rules are the structural checks that make geodesics and curvature computable.

title: Sphere Model: SO(3) Over SO(2)
notes: Anchor the abstraction in the round sphere. Rotations about the vertical axis fix the north pole and form k. The rotations that tip the pole form p, and their one-parameter orbits trace great circles. This example should make the symbols G, K, k, and p visible.

title: Geodesics Are Group Orbits
notes: Emphasize that the formula exp(tX).o is not a decorative notation choice. It says that a tangent vector in p is promoted to a one-parameter subgroup, and the subgroup moves the base point along a geodesic of the symmetric space.

title: The Exponential Differential Reads Curvature Sign
notes: Use the three rank-one curves as a distortion meter for normal coordinates. Positive curvature squeezes transverse variation through sin(r) over r, flat geometry leaves it unchanged, and negative curvature stretches it through sinh(r) over r. The same formal series knows all three cases.

title: Curvature Is A Bracket Measurement
notes: This slide is the algebraic center of the lecture. Once the symmetric pair is known, the curvature tensor at the base point is computed by a nested bracket. Students should read the sign comparison as evidence that geometry has been converted into Lie algebra bookkeeping.

title: Parallel Curvature Makes Local Data Portable
notes: Return to the local-to-global direction. Parallel curvature is what prevents the local model from changing as one moves. It lets the tangent-space curvature data act like a constant template, which is why the chapter can reconstruct a symmetric Lie algebra from one point.

title: Reconstructing A Model From One Tangent Space
notes: Explain the reconstruction as a disciplined build rather than magic. Start with p as the tangent space, add k as curvature-preserving endomorphisms, and define brackets so the curvature tensor becomes the p-p component. The Jacobi identity is the consistency test.

title: Compact Lie Groups Are Symmetric
notes: Compact Lie groups with bi-invariant metrics are not side examples; they demonstrate the general construction in a familiar algebraic setting. The product group G times G acts by left and right translation, the diagonal subgroup fixes the identity, and inversion supplies the point symmetry.

title: Locally Symmetric Versus Globally Symmetric
notes: Separate two claims that are easy to blur. Local symmetry is a differential condition visible in small neighborhoods, while global symmetry asks the point reflections to extend across the whole space. Completeness and simple connectedness are the bridge conditions that remove monodromy and boundary obstructions.

title: Lie Triple Systems Stay Totally Geodesic
notes: Introduce Lie triple systems as the tangent-space signature of a totally geodesic submanifold. The closure condition says that repeated curvature-style brackets never leave the chosen subspace. Geometrically, geodesics starting tangent to that subspace keep living inside the smaller symmetric piece.

title: Lab: Change The Curvature Sign
notes: Treat the lab as a controlled experiment. Changing one sign in the constant-curvature bracket changes the p-p bracket, the exponential distortion factor, and the curvature sign together. The value of the notebook is that these consequences can be checked independently and then recognized as one structure.

title: Recap: The Symmetry Pipeline
notes: Close by walking the pipeline from reflection to algebra and back to geometry. Local geodesic symmetries impose parallel curvature, global symmetries produce G over K, the involution gives k plus p, and the bracket formulas recover geodesics, curvature, compact group examples, and totally geodesic subspaces.
